title: #georgeclooney #georgeclooneybroadway #goodnightandgoodluck #goodnigh...
transcript: You might expect someone like George Clooney to make their Broadway debut in a super flashy role, but that's not the case here. Adapted from the film of the same name, Good Night, and Good Luck is a historical drama about journalist Edward R. Murrow going head to head with McCarthyisim and Senator Joseph McCarthy himself. I haven't seen the film, but I don't think it's required reading in order to understand this piece — in fact, the whole thing is almost overly obvious. But Clooney's performance is pretty subtle and understated. He does a great job of exuding a quiet stoicism, one that's not driven by ego, but by a self-assuredness and a calculated while knowingly imperfect faith in logic, reason, and his own moral compass. I’d venture to say that most audience members are just there to see George Clooney, and see him one does. But I also appreciated David Cromer's direction, which is similarly understated, with minimal frills, less one sequence of projections that I felt was groan-worthy in how on-the-nose it was. And that ties into my main critique of this piece, which is that it presents a lot of ideas and force feeds you how relevant they are, when the play's relevance could not be more obvious. It feels like hitting the nail on the head is the priority here, considering that in the play itself, there's not a whole lot of drama. There's a plot and it develops, but I was missing dramatic tension. And there are plenty of characters, but almost everyone other than Clooney exists just enough to establish time and place, rendering them somewhat underused. I still liked the piece despite finding it uneventful — it's just hard to ignore the price tag of these seats when evaluating it comprehensively. Clooney's performance is noteworthy, but it kind of exists as its own entity which I think could be better appreciated in a smaller space. But I guess it's not surprising that the demand to see George Clooney necessitates a big Broadway house. With that, another playbill for my collection.
reasoning: Reviewer praises Clooney's performance and Cromer's direction but criticizes the lack of dramatic tension, underused supporting characters, and heavy-handed messaging. The mention of the steep ticket price as a negative factor pushes this into clearly mixed territory.
